|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| add | int32 **15** | Q16.16 41 | float 129 | | 8.6× |
| mul | int32 **15** | Q15 34 | Q16.16 104 | float 162 | 10.8× |
| div | int32 **62** | float 457 | Q16.16 663 | | 10.7× |
| sin | Q15 table **58** | `f_sin` 1669 | `sinf` 2982 | | 51× |
| rot2d | Q15 **127** | Q16.16 447 | float 819 | | 6.5× |

sections.title: What Each Format Costs in Flash
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: What Each Format Costs in Flash
sections.body:
**`flashcost.py`**: script that attributes final linked flash bytes to routines.
**`nm`**: tool that lists linked symbols and their sizes.

Flash is another format budget.

Integer add/sub/multiply link no helpers.

Q15 sine 198 B, Q16 multiply 78, divide 604, int divide 470, float 4292, libm sine 4742.

Total image 27328 of 32768 bytes. Float+sinf around 9 KB exceeds a quarter of flash. nm --size-sort and flashcost.py count this ELF, with grouping choices for shared helpers.

Re-run after code/toolchain changes: library inclusion and sharing make these costs build-specific.

| format | brings in | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| int32 `+ − ×` | nothing — they are instructions | **0** |
| Q15 sine | `quarter[]` + `q15_sin` | **198** |
| Q16.16 multiply | `__aeabi_lmul` | **78** |
| Q16.16 divide | `__aeabi_ldivmod`, `__divdi3` … | **604** |
| int32 divide | `__aeabi_idiv` | **470** |
| float | `fadd fsub fmul fdiv`, compares, conversions | **4292** |
| libm `sinf` | `sinf`, kernels, `__kernel_rem_pio2f`, tables | **4742** |

sections.title: When Float Is Fine
sourceHeadings: Slide 18: When Float Is Fine
sections.body:
**`CPU`**: central processing unit.

Choose numeric format from rate×cost and accuracy, not speed ratios alone.

At 48 MHz float PI 784 cycles×500 Hz=392000 cycles/s=0.82%. Float FIR 4271×1000=8.9%.

Q15 FIR 302×1000=0.63%.

Hundreds-Hz application control can afford float and fmath.h for clarity. High-rate audio/current loops or tight flash may justify Q15.

Budget the whole loop and worst cases too, not just its arithmetic kernel.

Implementation / numeric example:

```
PI step, float   784 cycles x  500 Hz =   392 000 cycles/s =  0.82 % of the CPU
FIR16,   float  4271 cycles x 1000 Hz = 4 271 000 cycles/s =  8.9 %  of the CPU
FIR16,   Q15     302 cycles x 1000 Hz =   302 000 cycles/s =  0.63 % of the CPU
```

sections.title: Accuracy Against Cost
sourceHeadings: Slide 19: Accuracy Against Cost
sections.body:
**`dt`**: elapsed time per simulation or control update.

Quantized constants can dominate fixed-point error.

Q16 dt 0.01 becomes 655/65536≈0.009995, helping PI error reach 1.5e-4=9.5 LSB.

Integer FIR coefficients at 1/256 give 3.9e-3 full-scale error (8 LSB), while Q15 coefficients reduce it to 2.7e-5 (0.88 LSB), nearly as fast.

Host double-reference errors and modeled cycles in the table are distinct evidence.

Include representation of gains/time steps and output tolerance when comparing formats.

| job | format | max error | LSBs | cycles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mul | Q15 | 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.47 | 34 |
| mul | Q16.16 | 7.3 × 10⁻⁶ | 0.48 | 104 |
| rot2d | Q15 | 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.97 | 127 |
| rot2d | float | 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ | — | 819 |
| PI step | Q16.16 | 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ | **9.5** | 356 |
| fir16 | int32 (×256 coefficients) | 3.9 × 10⁻³ of full scale | **8.0** | 241 |
| fir16 | Q15 | 2.7 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.88 | 302 |

sections.title: DMA — a Second Bus Master
sourceHeadings: Slide 20: DMA — a Second Bus Master
sections.body:
**`ADC`**: analog-to-digital converter.
**`DMAMUX`**: DMA request multiplexer.
**`DR`**: data register.
**`EOC`**: end-of-conversion flag.

DMA is another bus master, transferring without CPU loads/stores.

ADC EOC requests flow through DMAMUX ID 5 to DMA channel 1, which copies DR into successive scan_buf slots.

C031 has one controller/three channels.

Requests, addresses, widths, increments and circular reload determine behavior. peripheral and memory must be configured coherently before enabling.

CPU can compute or sleep while acquisition proceeds.

sections.title: DMA and DMAMUX — Every Register on One Page
sourceHeadings: Slide 20b: DMA and DMAMUX — Every Register on One Page
sections.body:
**`overrun`**: new data arriving before the previous data was consumed.

**`ISR`**: interrupt service routine; in peripheral-register names, interrupt status register.
**`CPAR`**: DMA peripheral/source address register.
**`CMAR`**: DMA memory address register.
**`CNDTR`**: DMA transfer-count register.
**`CCR`**: configuration register; its meaning depends on the peripheral.

DMA1 base 0x40020000 has common ISR/IFCR and per-channel CCR/CNDTR/CPAR/CMAR spaced 0x14.

DMAMUX base 0x40020800 has C0–C2 request selectors.

AHBENR.DMA1EN gates both.

ISR has four flags/channel (global/complete/half/error).

IFCR write-one clears.

CCR declares widths/increments/direction/circular/priority/enable.

CNDTR counts transfers, CPAR source peripheral, CMAR memory.

DMAMUX sync/overrun and request generators exist but are unused here.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |

sections.body:
**`RAM`**: random-access memory.
**`MINC`**: memory address increment.
**`PINC`**: peripheral address increment.
**`CIRC`**: circular transfer reload.

Set CPAR=&ADC1->DR, CMAR=scan_buf, CNDTR=3, CCR=0x25A1.

PSIZE/MSIZE 01 mean 16-bit.

MINC steps RAM two bytes, PINC 0 keeps DR fixed.

CIRC reloads count/address.

DIR 0 peripheral-to-memory.

PL high.

CNDTR reports 3,2,1 as transfers progress.

Configure while disabled and enable last. Peripheral request must also be enabled.

Circular writes keep coming, so a reader needs coherent snapshot ownership when related samples matter.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
DMA1_Channel1->CPAR  = (uint32_t)&ADC1->DR;     /* from: the ADC result  */
DMA1_Channel1->CMAR  = (uint32_t)scan_buf;      /* to:   our array       */
DMA1_Channel1->CNDTR = 3;                       /* how many, then wrap   */
DMA1_Channel1->CCR   = DMA_CCR_PSIZE_0 | DMA_CCR_MSIZE_0 | DMA_CCR_MINC
                     | DMA_CCR_CIRC | DMA_CCR_PL_1 | DMA_CCR_EN;
```

sections.title: The ADC Side — Scan, Continuous, DMA
sourceHeadings: Slide 23b: The ADC Side — Scan, Continuous, DMA
sections.body:
CFGR1=0x2003 enables continuous conversions with circular DMA requests. CHSELR=0x13 selects channels IN0, IN1 and IN4. CHSELRMOD=0 and SCANDIR=0 make the ADC scan selected channels in ascending order. The buffer therefore receives X, Y and knob in that order, rather than the order in which software listed them.

At a 24 MHz ADC clock, 160.5 sampling cycles plus 12.5 processing cycles total 173 cycles. One conversion takes about 7.21 microseconds. Three conversions make a 21.6 microsecond scan, or roughly 46000 scans each second.

Polling all three results occupies about 1040 CPU cycles at 48 MHz. A DMA consumer reads the RAM buffer instead. These rates are calculated from the configuration; they are not observed Wokwi DMA transfers.

sections.title: Trust, But Watch — the Stuck-DMA Detector
sourceHeadings: Slide 24: Trust, But Watch — the Stuck-DMA Detector
sections.body:
**`RTC`**: real-time clock peripheral.

**`IWDG`**: independent watchdog.
**`PWR`**: power-control peripheral.

A runtime proof is needed before trusting unsupported hardware.

Wokwi's documented C031 model lacks DMA (also IWDG/PWR/RTC/SYSCFG/DBG).

Seed every ADC slot with **sentinel** 0xFFFF, outside the 12-bit range 0–4095, and bound the wait for all slots to change.

Failure stops scan and falls back to polled reads. A DMA-access HardFault reports its phase and USE_DMA 0 can skip it.

Predictions from RM0490/ST are not measurements.

Changing sentinel values proves writes occurred, not full sample coherence.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
for (i = 0; i < SCAN_CH; i++) scan_buf[i] = 0xFFFF;   /* a 12-bit ADC never writes this */
... start the ADC and the DMA ...
for (i = 0; i < SPIN_LIMIT; i++)
    if (scan_buf[0] != 0xFFFF && scan_buf[1] != 0xFFFF && scan_buf[2] != 0xFFFF)
        return 0;                                      /* proof: all three written      */
scan_stop();                                           /* never moved: undo, and say so */
return -1;
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```
  scan: DMA NEVER MOVED - buffer still 0xFFFF after the time limit.
        EXPECTED IN WOKWI: its C031C6 model does not implement DMA (docs.wokwi.com).
        On a real Nucleo this line says RUNNING.  Falling back to POLLED adc_read().
```

sections.body:
**`32-bit`**: occupying 32 binary digits, or four bytes.
**Flash memory** keeps program bytes without power.
**`overflow`**: a value or memory write exceeding the allocated range.
**`canary`**: known pattern checked for stack-boundary damage.

A selects an experiment, B runs it. Serial crash N and list provide the same control.

IDs 0–14 give fifteen selections, despite the source introduction's fourteen.

They cover mapped null reads, unaligned/wild/flash access, invalid callbacks, undefined/breakpoint instructions, stack overflow, hangs with interrupts on/off, starvation, a realistic bug, divide-zero and mystery faults.

sections.title: What the Core Does When Something Goes Wrong
sourceHeadings: Slide 2: What the Core Does When Something Goes Wrong
sections.body:
**`frame`**: saved register layout; in a communication context, one structured message.

**`MSP`**: main stack pointer.
**`PSP`**: process stack pointer.
**`xPSR`**: combined program status register.
**`lr`**: link register / return address.
**`pc`**: program counter / instruction address.
**`EXC_RETURN`**: exception-return encoding.

Hardware enters vector-table entry 3 after stacking r0, r1, r2, r3, r12, lr, pc and xPSR at frame offsets 0–28.

The stacked pc points at the faulting instruction or invalid target. lr is its caller return.

Handler lr contains EXC_RETURN: F9 indicates Thread/MSP and FD Thread/PSP. r4–r11 are still live registers, so save them before C reporting destroys evidence.

sections.title: One Handler, No Reasons
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: One Handler, No Reasons
sections.body:
**`BFAR`**: bus-fault address register on cores that provide it.
**`CFSR`**: configurable fault status register.
**`HFSR`**: HardFault status register.
**`MMFAR`**: memory-management fault address register.

ARMv6-M M0+ has only HardFault and no CFSR, HFSR, MMFAR or BFAR.

M3/M4/M7 provide those extra fault classes and reason/address registers.

Word/halfword misalignment faults here. Divide-zero has no hardware divide instruction to trap.

No stack-limit register exists.

MSPLIM arrives in ARMv8-M.

This lesson actually runs on M0+, superseding the earlier future-M4 promise.

Reconstruct causes from frame, instruction and map.

Factual reference:

| | Cortex-M0+ (this chip, Armv6-M) | Cortex-M3/M4/M7 (Armv7-M) |
|---|---|---|
| fault exceptions | **HardFault only** | HardFault, MemManage, BusFault, UsageFault |
| "why" register | **none** | `CFSR`, `HFSR` |
| "where" for a data fault | **none** | `MMFAR`, `BFAR` |
| unaligned word/halfword access | **always faults** | allowed (optional trap) |
| divide by zero | **no divide instruction** | `SDIV`/`UDIV`, optional trap |
| stack limit register | none | none (`MSPLIM` arrives in Armv8-M) |

sections.body:
**`RTOS`**: real-time operating system.
**`sp`**: stack pointer.

Decode state before memory. xPSR Thumb bit 24 clear suggests an even branch target. pc is then target and lr points after the call.

Exception number bits 5:0 nonzero indicate a fault inside a handler.

Padding bit 9 means pre-fault sp = frame + 32 + 4 = frame + 36 rather than frame + 32.

EXC_RETURN bit 2 selects MSP or PSP, so the wrapper also works with RTOS tasks.

Inspect lr when pc is an implausible target.

| `EXC_RETURN ; this lesson: main stack` | 32 = 0xFFFFFFF9 | 31:4 all ones, 3 Thread, 2 PSP, 1:0 |

sections.title: The Handler — Save First, Think Later
sourceHeadings: Slide 6: The Handler — Save First, Think Later
sections.body:
**`STM`**: store-multiple-registers instruction.

Naked assembly saves r4–r7, then moves r8–r11 through those low registers into crash_hi because Thumb-1 STM cannot name high registers. r0–r3 are usable scratch because hardware saved them.

Test EXC_RETURN bit 2, read MSP/PSP and pass frame plus return encoding to C.

C copies the record, safely reads instruction evidence, emits a line without printf and resets.

Calling C first can destroy the values needed for address reconstruction.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
__attribute__((naked)) void HardFault_Handler(void)
{
    __asm volatile(
        "   ldr   r3, =crash_hi      \n"
        "   stmia r3!, {r4-r7}       \n"     /* r4..r7                         */
        "   mov   r4, r8             \n"
        "   mov   r5, r9             \n"
        "   mov   r6, r10            \n"
        "   mov   r7, r11            \n"
        "   stmia r3!, {r4-r7}       \n"     /* r8..r11                        */
        "   movs  r0, #4             \n"
        "   mov   r1, lr             \n"
        "   tst   r0, r1             \n"     /* EXC_RETURN bit 2: which stack? */
        "   beq   1f                 \n"
        "   mrs   r0, psp            \n"
        "   b     2f                 \n"
        "1: mrs   r0, msp            \n"
        "2: mov   r1, lr             \n"     /* arg 2: EXC_RETURN              */
        "   ldr   r2, =crash_from_hardfault \n"
        "   bx    r2                 \n"
```

**`UDF`**: undefined-instruction trap.
**`BKPT`**: breakpoint instruction.

The saved registers let the decoder reconstruct an instruction's data address. Immediate offsets scale differently for word, halfword and byte instructions. Register-offset instructions add the saved base Rn and index Rm. Stack-relative instructions use the reconstructed pre-fault sp; literal loads use aligned pc+4.

For push and pop, count the registers and determine the memory span. Multiple-register transfers use base Rn. BX and BLX can reveal an invalid branch state, while UDF and BKPT identify deliberate traps.

Host comparison decoded 2327 relevant instructions from the ELF and matched objdump with zero mismatches. This checks the supported forms, not every instruction or target behavior.

Worked example: For LDR r2,[r3,#0], saved r3 is the address. An indexed instruction would also require its saved index or scaled immediate.

Factual reference:

| Encoding (hw) | Instruction | Address it touched |
|---|---|---|
| `0110 1 imm5 Rn Rt` | `ldr Rt, [Rn, #imm5*4]` | Rn + imm×4 |
| `0111 1 …` / `1000 1 …` | `ldrb` / `ldrh` | Rn + imm, Rn + imm×2 |
| `0101 opc Rm Rn Rt` | `str strh strb ldrsb ldr ldrh ldrb ldrsh` | Rn + Rm |
| `1001 L Rt imm8` | `ldr/str Rt, [sp, #imm8*4]` | sp + imm×4 |
| `01001 Rt imm8` | `ldr Rt, [pc, #imm8*4]` | Align(pc+4, 4) + imm×4 |
| `1011 010 M list` / `1011 110 P list` | `push` / `pop` | sp − 4n / sp |
| `1100 L Rn list` | `stmia` / `ldmia` | Rn |
| `0100 0111 L Rm 000` | `bx` / `blx Rm` | — a Thumb-bit suspect |
| `1101 1110 imm8` / `1011 1110 imm8` | `udf` / `bkpt` | — |

sections.title: The Verdict — Five Questions in Order
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: The Verdict — Five Questions in Order
sections.body:
**`GPIO`**: general-purpose input/output pins.
**`SRAM`**: static RAM.

Diagnose in order: Thumb state, executable pc, instruction decoding, alignment, mapped address span, and store permission.

Flash at 0x08000000 spans 32 KB plus boot alias. system memory is readable/executable.

SRAM at 0x20000000 spans 12 KB and is R/W/X.

Peripheral, GPIO and core-private regions are writable but **Execute Never**, which forbids instruction fetching.

0x60000000 is unmapped.

Validate pc before decoding so the diagnostic cannot fault while reading an invalid address.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
if (!(xpsr & (1UL << 24)))          return CAUSE_THUMB_BIT;     /* 1 */
if (!mem_can(pc, 2, MEM_X))         return CAUSE_BAD_FETCH;     /* 2 */
thumb_decode(hw1, hw2, pc, regs, &ins);                         /* 3 */
if (ins is udf / bkpt / svc)        return that;
if (addr & (size - 1))              return CAUSE_UNALIGNED;     /* 4 */
if (!mem_can(addr, span, MEM_R))    return CAUSE_BAD_ADDRESS;
if (store && region is read-only)   return CAUSE_READ_ONLY;     /* 5 */
```

Factual reference:

| Region | Range | R | W | X |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| flash (and its alias at 0) | `0x0800_0000` + 32 KB | ✓ | | ✓ |
| system memory | `0x1FFF_0000` | ✓ | | ✓ |
| SRAM | `0x2000_0000` + 12 KB | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| peripherals, GPIO | `0x4000_0000`, `0x5000_0000` | ✓ | ✓ | **never** |
| core private (SCB, NVIC, SysTick) | `0xE000_0000` | ✓ | ✓ | **never** |
| anything else | e.g. `0x6000_0000` | | | |

sections.title: Fault 1 — Unaligned
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: Fault 1 — Unaligned
sections.body:
A word load at words+1 targets 0x2000000D, not a multiple of four, so ARMv6-M faults.

The build's 9 B 01 loads r3 and 681 A loads through it. Host diagnosis reports the exact four-byte misalignment.

M4 can allow that access unless trapping is configured, so ported code may newly fail on M0+.

Byte access cannot misalign.

Renode incorrectly permits the access.

Wokwi behavior remains an exercise, with firmware reporting if no fault occurred.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
a = (uintptr_t)words + 1u;                  /* 1 byte into a word     */
sink = *(volatile uint32_t *)a;             /* LDR: Armv6-M faults    */
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```
80016ec:  9b01   ldr  r3, [sp, #4]      @ r3 = 0x2000000D
80016ee:  681a   ldr  r2, [r3, #0]      @ <- stacked pc: HardFault
```

sections.title: Faults 2 and 3 — Nothing There, or Read-Only
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: Faults 2 and 3 — Nothing There, or Read-Only
sections.body:
**`PGSERR`**: flash programming-sequence error flag.
**`WRPERR`**: flash write-protection error flag.
**`PROGERR`**: flash programming error flag.

A load from 0x60000000 touches no C031 resource and should HardFault. Reconstruct its address from r3 instead of BFAR.

A normal store to flash 0x08007F00 is not a programming operation: flash requires key/control sequence and a 64-bit program write.

Whether that store faults or returns with FLASH.SR errors is unobserved, so firmware supports both reports.

PGSERR, WRPERR and PROGERR plus alignment/size/busy fields explain refusal if execution continues.

The attempted flash payload is 0x12345678.

Correct programming uses FLASH->CR rather than an ordinary memory store.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `FLASH->SR` | 32 | 18 CFGBSY, 16 BSY1, 15 OPTVERR, 14 RDERR, 9 FASTERR, 8 MISERR, 7 PGSERR, 6 SIZERR, 5 PGAERR, 4 WRPERR, 3 PROGERR, 1 OPERR, 0 EOP |

sections.title: Faults 4 and 5 — Jumping Where Code Is Not
sourceHeadings: Slide 11: Faults 4 and 5 — Jumping Where Code Is Not
sections.body:
**`RCC`**: reset and clock control peripheral.

BLX through an unset callback r3=0 clears Thumb state.

Stacked pc=0 gives no useful call location, but lr=0x0800173B points immediately after the BLX at 0x08001738.

BLX to RCC|1 keeps Thumb set yet fetches at 0x40021000, an **Execute Never** region that forbids instruction fetching, producing a bad-fetch diagnosis.

Host frames verified both diagnostic paths.

An odd pointer preserves Thumb but does not establish executable or valid memory.

Implementation / numeric example:

```
8001734:  9301   str  r3, [sp, #4]      @ r3 = 0
8001736:  9b01   ldr  r3, [sp, #4]
8001738:  4798   blx  r3                @ branch to 0x00000000, bit 0 = 0
```

sourceHeadings: Slide 12: Faults 6 and 7 — and Two Things That Do Not Fault
sections.body:
UDF #11 (DE 0 B) is permanently undefined and used by deliberate traps.

BKPT (BE 11) halts with debugger attached but becomes HardFault without one on ARMv6-M.

Address-zero read aliases the flash vector's initial sp and returns 0x20003000. A NULL read can look valid while a NULL call clears Thumb.

Variable divide-zero calls this build's weak __aeabi_idiv0 and returns zero according to the traced listing, not an observed target run.

Define a policy override if needed.

```
800039e:  b501   push {r0, lr}
80003a0:  2000   movs r0, #0
80003a2:  f000   bl   80003b0 <__aeabi_idiv0>     @ 80003b0: 4770  bx lr
80003a6:  bd02   pop  {r1, pc}
```

sections.title: The Flight Recorder — RAM That Survives a Reset
sourceHeadings: Slide 13: The Flight Recorder — RAM That Survives a Reset
sections.body:
**`checksum`**: short value recomputed from message contents to detect some corruption.
**`NRST`**: external reset pin.

**`RAM`**: random-access memory.
**`XOR`**: exclusive OR, which keeps a bit when its inputs differ.
**`NOLOAD`**: linker section with no stored initialization payload.
**`noinit`**: RAM section intentionally skipped by startup initialization.

Ordinary reset restarts the core but does not clear SRAM. Startup copies data and zeroes bss.

A NOLOAD noinit section outside those ranges retains the 160-byte flight record through software/watchdog/NRST resets.

Power-on contents are garbage: trust only a valid magic and rotate-XOR checksum.

This build lays out noinit/stack around 0x200007E8, 0x20000C88 and end 0x20003000, with 9080 stack bytes.

Power loss and SRAM-losing modes invalidate retention.

Implementation / numeric example:

```
  .noinit (NOLOAD) : {
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _snoinit = .;
    *(.noinit) *(.noinit.*)
    . = ALIGN(4);
    _enoinit = .;
  } >RAM
```

sections.title: Why Did We Reset? Two Witnesses
sourceHeadings: Slide 14: Why Did We Reset? Two Witnesses
sections.body:
**`LSI`**: low-speed internal oscillator.

Read RCC.CSR2 once at boot, retain its sticky flags and clear through RMVF.

Reset flags distinguish low power, window/independent watchdog, software, power, pin and option-byte causes.

LSI enable/ready shares the register.

Firmware reset_why adds fault/canary/soft-dog/command detail before software reset, which RCC alone cannot distinguish.

Wokwi partial RCC may return impossible all-zero flags. Disclose model absence and use the validated noinit witness.

Static assertions check host flag copies against chip headers.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `RCC->CSR2 ; read once at boot, then RMVF` | 32 | 31 LPWR, 30 WWDG, 29 IWDG, 28 SFT, 27 PWR, 26 PIN, 25 OBL, 23 RMVF, 1 LSIRDY, 0 LSION |

sections.title: Stack Overflow — Nothing Faults
sourceHeadings: Slide 15: Stack Overflow — Nothing Faults
sections.body:
**`guard`**: protected memory boundary that blocks invalid accesses.

**`MPU`**: memory protection unit.

The stack grows down from 0x20003000 into ordinary writable heap/noinit/bss, so overflow need not fault.

Paint 0xDEADBEEF and check the bottom sixteen-word canary each loop.

Experiment 8 recurses 32 bytes below floor, returns and then triggers the check. Painting also provides a high-water mark.

C031 has an MPU, but a no-access guard can make HardFault entry itself push onto the failed stack and fault again into lockup.

Canary checking is delayed detection, not isolation.

Implementation / numeric example:

```
*** STACK OVERFLOW: the canary at _stack_floor is damaged - resetting
```

sections.title: The Watchdog — a Timer You Must Keep Resetting
sourceHeadings: Slide 16: The Watchdog — a Timer You Must Keep Resetting
sections.body:
**`ISR`**: interrupt service routine; in peripheral-register names, interrupt status register.
**`IWDG`**: independent watchdog.
**`WWDG`**: window watchdog.

A **watchdog** resets the system if meaningful progress stops refreshing its timer.

Ask who feeds and what it proves, what clocks the counter, and whether guarded code can disable it.

IWDG uses independent nominal 32 kHz LSI.

WWDG uses bus clock and a feeding window.

Both are irreversible until reset once started.

Timer-based software feeding cannot detect every failure: its clock and policy determine whether stopped work remains hidden.

sections.title: The IWDG — Four Keys
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: The IWDG — Four Keys
sections.body:
**`WINR`**: watchdog feed-window register.

**`PR`**: watchdog prescaler register.
**`RLR`**: watchdog reload register.

IWDG at 0x40003000 has KR keys, PR prescaler, twelve-bit RLR reload, SR update flags and optional WINR.

Start with CCCC, unlock with 5555, configure, wait boundedly for slow-domain updates and feed with AAAA.

Timeout=(RLR+1)*(4<<PR)/LSI.

PR=1 means divisor 8: RLR=3999 gives (3999+1)*8/32000=4000*8/32000, nominally one second at 32 kHz.

Range is 125 microseconds to 32.768 seconds, with oscillator tolerance.

Host picker checked each whole millisecond: finest fitting prescaler, never early and at most one tick late.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `IWDG->KR ; +0x00, write-only` | 32 | 15:0 KEY |
| `IWDG->PR ; +0x04, LSI / (4 << PR)` | 32 = 0x00000001 | 2:0 PR |
| `IWDG->RLR ; +0x08, counts RLR..0` | 32 = 0x00000F9F | 11:0 RL |
| `IWDG->SR ; +0x0C, update in progress` | 32 | 2 WVU, 1 RVU, 0 PVU |
| `IWDG->WINR ; +0x10, not used here` | 32 | 11:0 WIN |

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
IWDG->KR  = 0xCCCC;     /* start - and force the LSI on: irreversible */
IWDG->KR  = 0x5555;     /* unlock PR, RLR, WINR                       */
IWDG->PR  = pr;         /* LSI / (4 << pr)                            */
IWDG->RLR = rlr;        /* count rlr .. 0                             */
while (IWDG->SR & (IWDG_SR_PVU | IWDG_SR_RVU | IWDG_SR_WVU)) ;   /* bounded in wdog.c */
IWDG->KR  = 0xAAAA;     /* feed                                       */
```

Factual reference:

| Offset | Register | Its job | This lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | **`KR`** | write-only keys: start, unlock, feed | all three keys |
| 0x04 | **`PR`** | prescaler: LSI ÷ (4 << PR) | 1 for 1000 ms |
| 0x08 | **`RLR`** | reload: the count to restart from, 12 bits | 3999 for 1000 ms |
| 0x0C | **`SR`** | "an update to PR / RLR / WINR has not landed yet" | polled until 0 |
| 0x10 | `WINR` | window: a feed while the count is above it resets | — (left at reset value: off) |

sections.title: The WWDG — a Window, and a Shorter Reach
sourceHeadings: Slide 18: The WWDG — a Window, and a Shorter Reach
sections.body:
**`EWI`**: early-warning interrupt.

**`PCLK`**: peripheral bus clock.

WWDG at 0x40002C00 uses CR enable/counter, CFR prescaler/window/warning and SR warning.

Count transition 0x40 to 0x3F resets.

Clock=PCLK/(4096*2^WDGTB), so T=0x7F and prescaler 7 give 64*4096*128/48000000 = 699.05 ms maximum at 48 MHz.

A one-second request clamps.

Feeding while count remains above W also resets.

W=0x7F disables this early window.

EWI interrupts at 0x40, one tick before reset, permitting logging rather than general recovery.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `WWDG->CR ; +0x00, WDGA can be set, never cleared` | 32 = 0x000000FF | 7 WDGA, 6:0 T |
| `WWDG->CFR ; +0x04` | 32 = 0x0000387F | 13:11 WDGTB, 9 EWI, 6:0 W |
| `WWDG->SR ; +0x08, not used here` | 32 | 0 EWIF |

Implementation / numeric example:

```
WWDG clock = PCLK / (4096 × 2^WDGTB)          timeout = (T[5:0] + 1) / WWDG clock
```

Factual reference:

| Offset | Register | Its job | This lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | **`CR`** | on (`WDGA`), and the 7-bit down-counter `T` | written to arm, rewritten to feed |
| 0x04 | **`CFR`** | prescaler `WDGTB`, window `W`, early-warning enable `EWI` | `WDGTB`, `W = 0x7F` |
| 0x08 | `SR` | `EWIF`: the early warning fired | — (`EWI` stays off) |

sections.title: Feeding Honestly — the Heartbeat Bitmap
sourceHeadings: Slide 20: Feeding Honestly — the Heartbeat Bitmap
sections.body:
A **heartbeat bitmap** records completion of each required job. Blink runs every 250 ms, input every 10 ms and screen every 100 ms. A job sets its bit only after completing useful work.

Feed only when all required bits are present, then clear them for the next round. ISR-only or loop-only refresh cannot establish every job's progress.

If screen work starves while LEDs and serial remain active, its missing bit prevents refresh. Choose a timeout that covers the slowest healthy round plus any blocking work.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
if (wd_mode == WD_HEARTBEAT) { if (hb_ready(&hb)) { feed(); } }
```

sections.title: Measured — Who Feeds, Against What Failure
sourceHeadings: Slide 21: Measured — Who Feeds, Against What Failure
sections.body:
Host model steps at 1 ms with 250/10/100 ms jobs, 25 ms flush, one 180 ms print, timeout 1000 ms and failure at ten seconds.

Heartbeat hardware catches hang/IRQ-off at +750 ms and starvation at +1000. soft heartbeat misses IRQ-off.

Loop feeding misses starvation.

ISR feeding misses loop hangs and starvation while interrupts continue.

Only heartbeat with an independently counting watchdog covers all three modeled failure classes.

The full matrix is model evidence, not board observation.

Factual reference:

| fed by | dog | healthy | hang | hang, irq off | starve |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| heartbeat | soft | ok | +750 ms | **NEVER** | +1000 ms |
| heartbeat | WWDG/IWDG | ok | +750 ms | +750 ms | +1000 ms |
| every loop | soft | ok | +999 ms | NEVER | **NEVER** |
| every loop | WWDG/IWDG | ok | +999 ms | +999 ms | **NEVER** |
| SysTick ISR | soft | ok | **NEVER** | NEVER | NEVER |
| SysTick ISR | WWDG/IWDG | ok | **NEVER** | +999 ms | NEVER |

sections.title: How Tight Can the Timeout Be?
sourceHeadings: Slide 22: How Tight Can the Timeout Be?
sections.body:
Timeout must exceed worst healthy feeding gap plus margin.

Without a long print, host worst gap 275 ms needs 280 ms. A 180 ms report raises gap to 455 ms and safe timeout to 460 ms.

Modeled failure phases give 30/210 ms hang detection.

Polled UART at 115200 takes roughly 87 microseconds per character and extends loop deadlines.

Board stats measures actual worst gap. Five-minute exercise samples usage but cannot prove every unvisited path.

Factual reference:

| | worst feed gap | tightest safe timeout | a hang then caught in |
|---|---|---|---|
| no long prints | 275 ms | **280 ms** | 30 ms |
| with one 180 ms `report` | 455 ms | **460 ms** | 210 ms |

sections.title: The Post-Mortem of a Watchdog Reset
sourceHeadings: Slide 23: The Post-Mortem of a Watchdog Reset
sections.body:
Hardware watchdog reset invokes no logging handler, so continuously maintain last-loop and per-job timestamps in the retained record.

At boot compare age: stale loop with previously current jobs suggests hang. One stale job while loop stays fresh suggests starvation.

The displayed screen -1009 ms example is illustrative format output, not observed execution.

Reset flags and validated continuously maintained state jointly supply evidence. Do not expect last-moment code at a hardware reset.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
static void checkin(uint32_t bit, unsigned job)
{
    hb_checkin(&hb, bit);
    crash_rec.job_ms[job] = ms_now;
}
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```
---- a WATCHDOG reset us (armed: soft timeout 1000 ms) ----
  running: starve
  main loop's last pass at 14209 ms; last check-ins:  blink -59 ms  input -9 ms  screen -1009 ms
  diagnosis: a JOB stopped while the loop kept running (starved)
```

sections.title: Power — the Registers on One Page
sourceHeadings: Slide 24: Power — the Registers on One Page
sections.body:
**`ups`**: simulation updates per second.

**`SCB`**: System Control Block.
**`ICSR`**: interrupt control and state register.
**`SHPR3`**: system-handler priority register 3.
**`WFI`**: wait-for-interrupt instruction.
**`PWR`**: power-control peripheral.
**`CR1`**: control register 1.
**`SCR`**: system control register.
**`LPMS`**: low-power-mode selection field.

SCB at 0xE000ED00 controls core exceptions/reset/sleep.

PWR at 0x40007000 controls deep modes.

AIRCR keyed value 0x05FA0004 requests reset.

SCR selects deep sleep and exit behavior.

ICSR may reveal pending SysTick and SHPR3 places it at priority 3.

PWR CR1 LPMS bits 2:0 choose mode and flash power-down bits serve Sleep/Stop.

Wake/pull/status/backup registers are separate.

ARMv6-M alignment behavior is fixed, so layout labels do not imply M4-style optional unaligned permissions.

| `CPUID ; SCB +0x00, read-only` | 32 | 31:24 IMPLEMENTER, 23:20 VARIANT, 19:16 ARCHITECTURE, 15:4 PARTNO, 3:0 REVISION |

sections.title: WFI, and What Sleep Means on the C0
sourceHeadings: Slide 24b: WFI, and What Sleep Means on the C0
sections.body:
**`RTC`**: real-time clock peripheral.
**`BOR`**: brownout reset caused by low supply voltage.
**`WKUP`**: wake-up pin source.

**`LSE`**: low-speed external oscillator.

WFI enters ordinary Sleep when SLEEPDEEP=0. The CPU core stops, peripherals keep running, SRAM survives and an interrupt can wake it.

With SLEEPDEEP=1 and LPMS=000, Stop 0 keeps LSI/LSE and SRAM while EXTI can wake it. Standby uses LPMS=011, switches off the regulator and loses SRAM. WKUP, RTC, NRST, IWDG or BOR then wakes it as a reset.

Shutdown uses LPMS=100. Only LSE remains, SRAM is lost, and WKUP, RTC or NRST wakes it as a reset. Select the power mode and SLEEPDEEP before executing WFI. This lesson uses only ordinary Sleep; Wokwi cannot measure current or model these PWR modes.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `SCB->SCR ; 0 here: plain Sleep` | 32 = 0x00000000 | 4 SEVONPEND, 2 SLEEPDEEP, 1 SLEEPONEXIT |
| `PWR->CR1 ; used only when SLEEPDEEP = 1` | 32 | 5 FPD_SLP, 3 FPD_STOP, 2:0 LPMS |

Factual reference:

| Mode | How | Clocks | Exit | SRAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sleep** | `WFI`, `SLEEPDEEP = 0` | core stopped, peripherals running | any enabled interrupt | kept |
| **Stop 0** | `LPMS = 000`, `SLEEPDEEP = 1` | all stopped but LSI, LSE | an EXTI line | kept |
| **Standby** | `LPMS = 011` | all stopped but LSI, LSE; regulator off | WKUP pin, RTC, NRST, IWDG, BOR — as a **reset** | **lost** |
| **Shutdown** | `LPMS = 100` | all off but LSE | WKUP pin, RTC, NRST — as a **reset** | **lost** |

sections.title: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
sourceHeadings: Slide 28: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
sections.body:

sections.title: The SSD1306 — 1 KB of Picture at the End of Two Wires
sourceHeadings: Slide 3: The SSD1306 — 1 KB of Picture at the End of Two Wires
sections.body:
SSD1306 holds its own picture RAM and refreshes the OLED independently.

Address is 0x3C by default, sometimes 0x3D.

A 128×64 image has 8192 bits=1024 bytes, arranged as eight pages of 128 vertical eight-pixel strips with least-significant bit at the top.

MCU transfers picture bytes rather than refreshing every visible pixel continuously.

A **dirty page** has changed since its last successful transfer; pages are the natural transfer unit.

sourceHeadings: Slide 4: A Pixel Is a Bit — Which Byte, Which Bit

sections.title: The SSD1306 — Everything It Understands, on One Page
sourceHeadings: Slide 5: The SSD1306 — Everything It Understands, on One Page
sections.body:
**`Co`**: SSD1306 continuation-control bit.
**`D/C#`**: SSD1306 data-versus-command control bit.
**`charge pump`**: panel circuit that generates the voltage needed to light the OLED.

**`I2C`**: Inter-Integrated Circuit two-wire bus.
**`NOP`**: no-operation command.

SSD1306 interface comprises control byte, picture RAM and command/parameter stream rather than MCU-style addressed registers.

Control bit 6 selects data. Commands set display/pump/contrast/orientation and address windows.

Opcode bits distinguish off/on, normal/inverted and remapped scan direction.

Addressing mode bits 1:0 select horizontal 00, vertical 01, page 10. Window columns use 7 bits and page uses 3.

Init uses the complete listed command set. Scrolling/page-mode/NOP alternatives are unused.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `control ; 0x40: pixel data follows` | 8 = 0x40 | 7 Co, 6 D/C#, 5:0 |
| `AE / AF ; display off / on` | 8 = 0xAF | 7:1, 0 ON |
| `A6 / A7 ; normal / inverted` | 8 = 0xA6 | 7:1, 0 INVERT |
| `A0 / A1 ; segment remap` | 8 = 0xA1 | 7:1, 0 REMAP |
| `C0 / C8 ; COM scan direction` | 8 = 0xC8 | 7:4, 3 DOWN, 2:0 |
| `40 ; display start line` | 8 = 0x40 | 7:6, 5:0 LINE |
| `8D, then ; charge pump parameter` | 8 = 0x14 | 4, 2 ENABLE |
| `20, then ; addressing mode: 00 horiz, 01 vert, 10 page` | 8 = 0x00 | 1:0 MODE |
| `21, then a ; first column` | 8 = 0x00 | 6:0 START |
| `21, then b ; last column` | 8 = 0x7F | 6:0 END |
| `22, then a ; first page` | 8 | 2:0 START |
| `22, then b ; last page` | 8 | 2:0 END |

Factual reference:

| Byte(s) | What it is | This lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `00` / `40` | **control byte**: commands follow / pixels follow | first byte of every transfer |
| RAM | **8 pages × 128 bytes**, a byte is a column of 8 pixels | written one page at a time |
| `AE` / `AF` | display off / on | off to configure, on last |
| `D5` *x* | clock divide, oscillator | `80`, the default |
| `A8` *x* | multiplex ratio = rows − 1 | `3F`: 64 rows |
| `D3` *x* | vertical display offset | `00` |
| `40`–`7F` | display start line (low 6 bits) | `40`: line 0 |
| **`8D`** *x* | **charge pump** | **`14`: on** |
| **`20`** *x* | **memory addressing mode** | `00`: horizontal |
| **`21`** *a b* | **column window**, start and end | `0`, `127` |
| **`22`** *a b* | **page window**, start and end | `p`, `p` |
| `A0` / `A1` | segment remap | `A1`: x left → right |
| `C0` / `C8` | COM scan direction | `C8`: y top → bottom |
| `DA` *x* | COM pin layout | `12`, for 64 rows |
| `81` *x* | contrast | `CF`; `oled_contrast()` |
| `D9` *x* · `DB` *x* | pre-charge period · VCOMH level | `F1` · `40` |
| `A4` / `A5` | show RAM / all pixels on | `A4` |
| `A6` / `A7` | normal / inverted | `A6`; `oled_invert()` |
| — | scrolling (`26`–`2F`, `A3`), page-mode addressing (`00`–`1F`, `B0`–`B7`), NOP (`E3`) | not used |

sections.title: Every Write Starts With a Control Byte
sourceHeadings: Slide 5b: Every Write Starts With a Control Byte
sections.body:
After I²C address, control 0x00 means commands and 0x40 means pixel data.

D/C# bit 6 distinguishes them.

Co bit 7 clear means remaining bytes keep the same kind.

Each RAM page has 129 bytes: permanent 0x40 prefix plus 128 pixels.

Sending this page directly avoids copying into another transmit buffer.

Eight prefixed pages occupy 1032 bytes, slightly more than the 1024 picture payload.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `control ; 0x00: commands follow` | 8 = 0x00 | 7 Co, 6 D/C#, 5:0 |
| `control ; 0x40: pixel data follows` | 8 = 0x40 | 7 Co, 6 D/C#, 5:0 |

Implementation / numeric example:

```
S | 0x3C+W | A | 0x00 | A | cmd | A | cmd ... | P        commands
S | 0x3C+W | A | 0x40 | A | px  | A | px  ... | P        128 pixel bytes
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
static uint8_t fb[OLED_PAGES][1 + OLED_W];  /* [0] = 0x40, then 128 */
```

sections.title: Bringing the Panel Up — 16 Commands
sourceHeadings: Slide 6: Bringing the Panel Up — 16 Commands
sections.body:
**`ACK`**: acknowledgment.

Keep the panel off while configuring it. Send D5 80 for oscillator/clock, A8 3F for a 64-row multiplex ratio, D3 00 for zero offset and 40 for the starting line. Enable the charge pump with 8D 14 and horizontal addressing with 20 00.

Configure remapping with A1 and scan direction with C8. Use DA 12 for pins, 81 CF for contrast, D9 F1 for precharge and DB 40 for VCOMH. Select display from RAM with A4, normal pixels with A6, then turn the display on with AF.

These sixteen command transfers followed by clearing eight pages produced 32 host-counted transfers and 1161 bytes. A missing charge-pump setting can leave the display dark even while it acknowledges writes.

The values match a common 128x64 internal-pump setup, but counting output does not prove target acceptance. Adafruit's comparison initialization also sends 0x2E to stop scrolling; scrolling is already off after reset here.

Factual reference:

| Bytes | Command | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `AE` | display off | configure in the dark |
| `D5 80` | clock divide | the default |
| `A8 3F` | multiplex 64 | this panel has 64 rows |
| `D3 00` · `40` | offset 0, start line 0 | |
| **`8D 14`** | **charge pump on** | **without it the panel stays dark** |
| `20 00` | horizontal addressing | column, then page — the relevant section |
| `A1` · `C8` | segment remap, COM scan down | x left→right, y top→bottom |
| `DA 12` | COM pin layout | for 64 rows |
| `81 CF` · `D9 F1` · `DB 40` | contrast, pre-charge, VCOMH | |
| `A4` · `A6` · `AF` | show RAM, not inverted, **on** | |

sections.title: I2C1 — the MCU's Side of the Wire, on One Page
sourceHeadings: Slide 7: I2C1 — the MCU's Side of the Wire, on One Page
sections.body:
**`STOPF`**: I2C stop-detected flag.
**`SMBus`**: System Management Bus extension of I2C.

**`CPU`**: central processing unit.
**`ISR`**: interrupt service routine; in peripheral-register names, interrupt status register.
**`ICR`**: interrupt clear register.
**`CR1`**: control register 1.
**`CR2`**: control register 2.
**`PE`**: peripheral enable bit.
**`TIMINGR`**: I2C timing register.
**`TXDR`**: I2C transmit data register.
**`RXDR`**: I2C receive data register.

I2C1 at 0x40005400 reuses the polled driver.

CR1/TIMINGR set PE and bus timing 0x0090273D while disabled.

CR2 declares shifted address, count, direction, start/end.

ISR requests bytes or reports terminal/error.

ICR clears sticky events.

TXDR/RXDR carry payload.

Panel never sends measurement data, so RXDR is unused here.

OAR/SMBus fields are unused, while software timeout/error cleanup remain essential.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `CR1 ; control` | 32 | 7 ERRIE, 6 TCIE, 5 STOPIE, 4 NACKIE, 2 RXIE, 1 TXIE, 0 PE |
| `CR2 ; one transfer, 7-bit address in 7:1` | 32 | 26 PECBYTE, 25 AUTOEND, 24 RELOAD, 23:16 NBYTES, 15 NACK, 14 STOP, 13 START, 12 HEAD10R, 11 ADD10, 10 RD_WRN, 9:8, 7:1 SADD, 0 |
| `TIMINGR ; bus speed` | 32 = 0x0090273D | 31:28 PRESC, 23:20 SCLDEL, 19:16 SDADEL, 15:8 SCLH, 7:0 SCLL |
| `ISR ; status` | 32 | 15 BUSY, 7 TCR, 6 TC, 5 STOPF, 4 NACKF, 3 ADDR, 2 RXNE, 1 TXIS, 0 TXE |
| `ICR ; clear flags` | 32 | 5 STOPCF, 4 NACKCF, 3 ADDRCF |
| `RXDR ; received byte` | 32 | 7:0 RXDATA |
| `TXDR ; byte to send` | 32 | 7:0 TXDATA |

Factual reference:

| Offset | Register | Its job | `i2c.c` here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x00 | **`CR1`** | enable, interrupts, filters | `PE` = 0, then 1 around `TIMINGR` |
| 0x04 | **`CR2`** | one transfer: address, direction, count, start / stop | `SADD`, `RD_WRN`, `NBYTES`, `AUTOEND`, `START`, `STOP` |
| 0x08, 0x0C | `OAR1`, `OAR2` | the MCU's own address, as a target | — |
| 0x10 | **`TIMINGR`** | SCL high / low times: the bus speed | `0x0090273D` once |
| 0x14 | `TIMEOUTR` | SMBus timeouts | — |
| 0x18 | **`ISR`** | status flags, polled | `TXIS`, `RXNE`, `TC`, `STOPF`, `NACKF` |
| 0x1C | **`ICR`** | write 1 to clear a flag | `STOPCF`, `NACKCF` |
| 0x20 | `PECR` | SMBus packet error check | — |
| 0x24 | **`RXDR`** | the byte received | read (MPU6050, not the panel) |
| 0x28 | **`TXDR`** | the next byte to send | each of the 7 + 129 bytes |

sections.title: Sending One Page
sourceHeadings: Slide 7b: Sending One Page
sections.body:
**`AUTOEND`**: automatic STOP after the declared byte count.
**`NBYTES`**: transaction payload byte count.

For each dirty page, command stream sets columns 0–127 with 21 and page p–p with 22, then sends control 40 and 128 data bytes.

Horizontal mode automatically increments columns.

Address 0x3C shifts to 0x78.

CR2 window transfer 0x02072078 has 7 bytes, page 0x02812078 has 129 and AUTOEND.

Eight-bit NBYTES limits ordinary single transfer to 255 bytes: a page fits, a 1024-byte screen would need reload or splitting.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
const uint8_t win[6] = {0x21, 0, OLED_W - 1, 0x22, (uint8_t)p, (uint8_t)p};
int rc = command(win, sizeof win);
if (rc == 0) { rc = i2c_write_read(OLED_ADDR, fb[p], 1u + OLED_W, 0, 0); }
```

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `I2C1->CR2 ; the window: 0x00 + 6 command bytes` | 32 = 0x02072078 | 26, 25 AUTOEND, 24, 23:16 NBYTES, 15, 14, 13 START, 12, 11, 10 RD_WRN, 9:8, 7:1 SADD, 0 |
| `I2C1->CR2 ; the page: 0x40 + 128 pixel bytes` | 32 = 0x02812078 | 26, 25 AUTOEND, 24, 23:16 NBYTES, 15, 14, 13 START, 12, 11, 10 RD_WRN, 9:8, 7:1 SADD, 0 |

sections.title: The Bus Budget — Arithmetic Before Code
sourceHeadings: Slide 8: The Bus Budget — Arithmetic Before Code
sections.body:
An I2C byte needs nine clocks including its acknowledgment. At 400 kHz that is 22.5 microseconds per byte. A page needs the window address/control/six commands plus pixel address/control/128 data bytes, totaling 138 wire bytes. With modeled start/stop overhead, that is about 3.12 ms.

All eight pages total 1104 bytes and about 24.9 ms. A 50 Hz simulation update has a 20 ms budget, so a full repaint already exceeds it before computation. The polled driver also occupies the CPU during that transfer.

The earlier AVR parallel display needed 14 microseconds per byte, or 14.3 ms for a full picture. That uses a different trade between pins and time. Measure actual TIMINGR rate and firmware overhead on the target; the 400 kHz arithmetic is a model.

Factual reference:

| One page | Bytes on the wire | Bits | Time at 400 kHz |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| window: address + `00` + 6 | 8 | 72 + START/STOP | 0.19 ms |
| pixels: address + `40` + 128 | 130 | 1 170 + START/STOP | 2.93 ms |
| **one page** | **138** | | **3.12 ms** |
| **all 8 pages** | **1 104** | | **24.9 ms** |

sections.title: The Framebuffer and Dirty Pages
sourceHeadings: Slide 9: The Framebuffer and Dirty Pages
sections.body:
**`dirty bit`**: flag saying a display page changed and still needs transfer.
**`ownership`**: rule determining which component may use or modify a resource.

Drawing modifies the RAM framebuffer; a flush copies changed pages to the panel.

A one-byte bitmap marks pages only when a byte changes. flush sends marked pages and clears each bit only after success.

Failed pages remain dirty for retry.

Clearing an already-blank page changes nothing, so no transfer.

Prefixed framebuffer 1032 bytes is about 8% of 12 KB RAM versus 25% of AVR 4 KB.

This is transfer ownership/error state as well as optimization.

sections.title: The Trap — Clear, Then Redraw Everything
sourceHeadings: Slide 10: The Trap — Clear, Then Redraw Everything
sections.body:
**`frame`**: saved register layout; in a communication context, one structured message.
**`overflow`**: a value or memory write exceeding the allocated range.

Clear-then-redraw defeats dirty tracking because intermediate erasure dirties every occupied page even if final pixels match.

Host SNAKE clear/redraw averaged 970 bytes versus 129 for differential drawing.

Save last-drawn positions, erase all moved objects first, then draw their new positions so erasure cannot cut newly drawn objects.

SNAKE tracks up to eight changed cells. Overflow requests a full repaint.

Dirty-per-write tracking cannot detect equal net pictures without another comparison strategy.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
static void mark(int c)
{
    if (n_changed < 8) { changed[n_changed++] = (uint16_t)c; }
    else               { need_full = 1; }     /* too many: repaint all */
}
```

Factual reference:

| Strategy | Pages dirty per SNAKE frame |
|---|---|
| clear + redraw everything | every page anything is drawn on — the wall alone is in all 7 below the HUD. **Measured on the host: 970 B per frame**, 88 % of a full repaint |
| **erase what moved, draw what moved** | the new head, the old tail, maybe an apple: 1–3 pages. **Measured: 129 B per frame** |

**`ups`**: simulation updates per second.

FLAP pipes span height and move each tick;81% of its frames exceed 20 ms, so differential rendering gains little.

Fixed-step updates keep physics/replay independent of render time. Variable dt can enlarge collisions enough to tunnel and differ across devices.

If updates themselves exceed 20 ms, unlimited catch-up work creates a spiral where catching up adds more delay.

MAX_CATCHUP 4 drops lost time and permits rendering.

sections.title: A Microsecond Stopwatch, Free, From SysTick
sourceHeadings: Slide 14: A Microsecond Stopwatch, Free, From SysTick
sections.body:
**`SysTick`**: core countdown timer used for ticks.
**`VAL`**: SysTick current counter value.
**`LOAD`**: SysTick reload value.

SysTick CTRL 7 enables core clock/IRQ/counter.

LOAD 47999 (0xBB7F) wraps every millisecond at 48 MHz.

VAL downcount gives fractional microseconds=(LOAD-VAL)/48.

Read ms, VAL, then ms again and retry if changed to avoid torn software-time samples.

A pending-but-not-serviced rollover is an additional implementation limitation if interrupts are masked. Do not claim the simple retry solves every timer race.

PERF reports fps, ups, flush_us, max_us, bytes/frame, busy%, mode once per second.

Bit-field reference (inclusive positions):

| Register or encoding | Width / value | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| `SysTick->CTRL ; SysTick_Config(): core clock, IRQ, on` | 32 = 0x00000007 | 16 COUNTFLAG, 2 CLKSOURCE, 1 TICKINT, 0 ENABLE |
| `SysTick->LOAD ; 48 000 - 1: one wrap per ms` | 32 = 0x0000BB7F | 31:24, 23:0 RELOAD |
| `SysTick->VAL ; counts down 47 999 → 0, read by now_us()` | 32 | 31:24, 23:0 CURRENT |

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
static uint32_t now_us(void)
{
    uint32_t m, v;
    do {                     /* ms ticked while we read VAL? again */
        m = ms;
        v = SysTick->VAL;
    } while (m != ms);
    return m * 1000u + (SysTick->LOAD - v) / (SystemCoreClock / 1000000u);
}
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```
$PERF,<fps>,<ups>,<flush_us>,<max_us>,<bytes/frame>,<busy %>,<DIRTY|FULL>*CS
```

sections.title: One Loop, or the RTOS?
sourceHeadings: Slide 15: One Loop, or the RTOS?
sections.body:
**`preemption`**: interrupting a task to let a more urgent task run.
**`mutex`**: exclusive resource lock that can block competing tasks.

**`RTOS`**: real-time operating system.

A single-owner game pipeline input→update→draw→flush suits a superloop with next+=20 and WFI.

RTOS splitting would introduce shared framebuffer synchronization or a second 1 KB buffer while flush must not overlap drawing.

Deterministic replay also becomes harder with arbitrary preemption.

Multiple independent deadlines justify tasks: a drone's fast motor/attitude loop must preempt a 25 ms low-priority display flush, ideally page by page.

Architecture follows deadlines and ownership.

Factual reference:

| | Superloop (this lesson) | RTOS tasks |
|---|---|---|
| work to do | one chain: input → update → draw → flush | separate activities with separate deadlines |
| shared data | none — one thread owns everything | the framebuffer, touched by update/draw *and* flush |
| what tasks would need | — | a mutex or a second 1 KB buffer, or the flush sends a half-drawn frame (lesson 03's tearing, on glass) |
| timing | `next += 20` and `__WFI()` | `os_delay_until()` — the same idea |
| determinism | the host test replays it exactly | preemption points vary run to run |

sections.title: Input — Levels, Edges and Zones
sourceHeadings: Slide 16: Input — Levels, Edges and Zones
sections.body:
**`dead zone`**: small central input range treated as zero to suppress noise.

**`ADC`**: analog-to-digital converter.
**`pressed`**: new button-press edge.

After two agreeing debounce samples, pressed=now&~stable, released=stable&~now, down=now.

FLAP/serve use edge so holding does not trigger 50 times/s.

SNAKE uses stronger-axis level past 35%. Menu uses crossings of ±50% zones.

ADC stick scales -100…100 with dead zone and horizontal polarity flips Wokwi's right=0 V into positive-right convention. pressed lasts one pad_read, so sample every update, not merely every rendered frame.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
p->pressed  = (uint8_t)(now & ~stable);   /* went down since the last read */
p->released = (uint8_t)(stable & ~now);   /* came up                       */
p->down     = now;                        /* held                          */
```

Factual reference:

| Action | Uses | Why |
|---|---|---|
| FLAP's flap | `pressed` | holding the button must not flap 50 times a second |
| BREAKOUT's serve | `pressed` | |
| SNAKE's steering | stick **level**, larger axis past 35 % | a held direction is a held intention |
| menu up / down | stick **zone edge** | crossing ±50 % once = one step |

sections.title: Sprites — and Why `const` Is Enough on ARM
sourceHeadings: Slide 17: Sprites — and Why `const` Is Enough on ARM
sections.body:
**Flash memory** keeps program bytes without power.

**`LSB`**: least-significant bit or one raw numeric step.

Sprites share panel format: one byte/column, LSB top.

Bird has two 8×6 frames. column 2's lit bits 0,2,5 form 0x25.

ASCII sprite tool converts artwork to columns.

ARM's unified address space lets ordinary loads read const .rodata in flash.

AVR requires PROGMEM/pgm_read_byte.

Forgetting const copies tables into RAM at boot without obvious behavior failure.

Whole arcade data+bss 2712 B versus AVR 1372.

ARM 12 KB makes framebuffer about 8% instead of 25%.

Implementation / numeric example:


sections.title: Physics in Two Lines — and Fixed Point
sourceHeadings: Slide 18: Physics in Two Lines — and Fixed Point
sections.body:
FLAP stores vertical position and velocity in units of 1/256 pixel. Every 20 ms update adds 28 to vy, then adds vy to by. This models gravity of about 273 pixels/s². A flap sets vy to -400, about -78 pixels/s.

After hovering until tick 150, the falling displacement after n steps is 28*n*(n+1)/(2*256). Falling 27 pixels needs n*(n+1)>=494, so n=22. The implementation's host check reaches death at tick 171.

The original whole-pixel paddle calculation x*4/100 discarded stick inputs below 25% on every update. Keeping a fractional position lets those small increments accumulate. Integer division truncates toward zero, whereas an arithmetic right shift can round negative values downward.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
vy += GRAVITY;          /* 28/256 px per tick^2   = 273 px/s^2 */
by += vy;               /* a flap SETS vy = -400  = -78 px/s   */
```

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
pxf += (int32_t)in->x * (4 << FP) / 100;    /* in 1/256 px */
px   = (int)(pxf >> FP);
```

sections.title: Collision — Four Comparisons
sourceHeadings: Slide 19: Collision — Four Comparisons
sections.body:
**`AABB`**: axis-aligned bounding box.

AABB overlap requires both horizontal and vertical intervals to overlap, with strict comparisons excluding mere touching.

FLAP shrinks its bird box by one pixel for forgiving corners.

BREAKOUT compares prior ball position to pick top/bottom versus side bounce, flipping vy or vx.

Paddle hit offset controls angle from straight upward at center to 45 degrees at ends.

Keeping travel below small obstacle scales reduces tunneling. The source uses below 3 pixels/tick for its 3-pixel bricks and 2-pixel paddle/ball.

A strict guarantee requires swept/relative-bound analysis.

Worked example: A ball previously within a brick's columns entered from above/below, so reverse vy. Otherwise it crossed a side, so reverse vx.

Implementation / numeric example:

```c
static inline int aabb(int ax, int ay, int aw, int ah,
                       int bx, int by, int bw, int bh)
{
    return ax < bx + bw && bx < ax + aw && ay < by + bh && by < ay + ah;
}
```

sourceHeadings: Slide 21: Sound — a Sequencer on a Timer
sections.body:
TIM3 PWM at 1 MHz sustains tones without CPU: ARR+1=1000000/frequency and CCR1 half the period.

440 Hz needs ARR=2272.

Effect tables pair frequency/duration, zero Hz means rest and zero duration ends. sound_poll advances on deadlines. Games only invoke sfx, replaced by event counters in host tests.

The retained eat/over/high tables show their exact sequences.

A 25 ms polled flush can extend notes by up to that delay. Interrupt sequencing instead needs shared-state synchronization.

sections.title: SNAKE
sourceHeadings: Slide 22: SNAKE
sections.body:
SNAKE packs 403 cells as sixteen-bit cy*31+cx ring entries (806 bytes) plus 51-byte occupancy bitmap.

Push-head/pop-tail and membership checks are constant time.

Entering the old tail is legal only when it vacates, not when growing. Test before mutating so a fatal move does not shorten the body.

Every fifth apple shortens period one tick. Levels start at eight to four ticks/move.

Host level 3 ate 42 apples in 58.7 seconds: length 87, score 126.

No-input wall death tick 126 equals 21 moves times six ticks.

The example host captures were taken at SNAKE tick 2000, BREAKOUT tick 900 and FLAP tick 700. Those labels locate pictures and do not add separate game timing guarantees.

sections.title: BREAKOUT
sourceHeadings: Slide 23: BREAKOUT
sections.body:
BREAKOUT stores 48 bricks in four sixteen-bit row words.

Column bits permit cheap test and AND-clearing. All zero ends a wave.

Top rows and higher levels score more, paddle narrows from 20 pixels at level 1 to 12 at level 5, and later waves speed up.

Host level-3 autopilot predicted landing and played five minutes: 188 bricks, three waves, score 1395, no lost ball.

No input automatically serves after three seconds and ends after three misses on tick 599.

These validate hardware-independent game behavior, not target playability.

sections.title: FLAP
sourceHeadings: Slide 24: FLAP
sections.body:
FLAP recycles three pipes: a departing one returns 156 pixels to the right with a random gap.

Gap narrows from 26 pixels at level 1 to 18 at level 5. Pace increases every five pipes.

Host level-3 autopilot passed 97 pipes in 71 seconds, flapping when feet came within three pixels of gap bottom.

A middle-gap trigger scored only 20 because a flap climbs about eleven pixels and hits the upper pipe.

Design input policy from predicted dynamics.

sections.title: The Arcade — a State Machine
sourceHeadings: Slide 25: The Arcade — a State Machine
sections.body:
In MENU, A enters PLAY. B toggles PLAY/PAUSE. Game completion enters OVER and emits one SCORE record.

In OVER, A restarts the same game with a new seed; B returns to MENU. Ignore input for 0.75 seconds after losing so the press that caused the loss cannot also dismiss the result.

Keep the high score and blink NEW HIGH with XOR drawing; applying the same XOR twice restores the background. Emit SCORE on state entry and handle input edges to avoid repeated scores.

sections.title: `$SCORE` — a Class Leaderboard With a Checksum
sourceHeadings: Slide 26: `$SCORE` — a Class Leaderboard With a Checksum
sections.body:
**`checksum`**: short value recomputed from message contents to detect some corruption.

**`MAC`**: message authentication code.

score_frame emits checked printable $SCORE,SNAKE,172*2E.

Leaderboard consumes one captured file per player, rejects wrong XOR and lists top ten per game.

Host-valid output passed. An altered digit failed.

This catches copying/truncation accidents but equal-bit changes can cancel and a fabricated score can be correctly checksummed.

Authenticating a sender requires a MAC and secret-key management, beyond the honest-player classroom challenge.

Implementation / numeric example:

```
$SCORE,SNAKE,172*2E
```

Factual reference:

| Catches | Misses |
|---|---|
| a digit mistyped while copying | a score made up and checksummed by hand |
| a truncated line | two errors that cancel in the XOR |

sections.title: What the Host Test Proves
sourceHeadings: Slide 27: What the Host Test Proves
sections.body:
Host GCC compiles five game files and actual OLED/protocol implementations.

Twenty checks cover growth/scoring, no-input deaths at ticks 126/599/171, replay hashes/new seed, bricks/pipes, 129-versus-1104-byte dirty savings, 24.92 ms full-flush budget, menu/high-score/checksum.

Failure exits nonzero and captures produce ASCII/SVG images.

Host checks cannot establish SSD1306 acceptance, physical I²C timing, input focus or playability.

Factual reference:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| SNAKE eats, grows by 2 per apple, scores level × apples | 42 apples, length 87, score 126 |
| SNAKE with no input dies on the predicted tick | 126 |
| same seed + inputs → same framebuffer hash; new seed → different | ✓ |
| BREAKOUT breaks bricks, score rises | 188 bricks, 3 waves |
| BREAKOUT with no input: auto-serve, 3 misses, game over | tick 599 |
| FLAP passes pipes | 97 |
| FLAP with no input falls on the predicted tick | 171 |
| dirty pages cut SNAKE's bus bytes by > 4× | 129 vs 1 104 B |

sections.title: Flash and RAM
sourceHeadings: Slide 28: Flash and RAM
sections.body:
**`nm`**: tool that lists linked symbols and their sizes.

**`ELF`**: executable file containing linked code, addresses and symbols.

This ELF reports text 14092, rodata 1568, data 132, bss 2580 and stack/heap reservation 1536 bytes.

Flash includes data's initial values: 15980/32768=48.8%.

Runtime RAM is data+bss+reservation=4248/12288=34.6%.

Font 475 bytes, framebuffer 1032 and snake ring 806 explain major data costs. printf helpers total 1568 bytes, larger than breakout_step at 752.

Re-measure with size/nm after changes. These are build-specific capacities.

Startup copies .data initial values from flash to writable RAM, so both budgets include them.

Factual reference:

| Section | Bytes | What |
|---|---:|---|
| `.text` | 14 092 | code: three games, menu, engine, oled, i2c, pad, adc, beep, printf |
| `.rodata` | 1 568 | the font (475 B), sprites, note tables, strings |
| `.data` | 132 | initialised variables |
| `.bss` | 2 580 | framebuffer 1 032, snake ring 806, the rest |
| stack + heap | 1 536 | reserved by the linker script |

sections.title: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
sourceHeadings: Slide 29: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
sections.body:
Host real-code results count SNAKE 129, BREAKOUT 220, FLAP 935 and full 1104 bus bytes per frame.

A 400 kHz model predicts full 24.92 ms, page 3.1 ms and 50 updates/s with 40.1 full-repaint frames/s.

Nothing ran in Wokwi: actual polled flush time/TIMINGR rate, OLED init/page acceptance, update/draw CPU load, button focus and playability remain open.

PERF flush_us and busy measurements investigate the target.

Counted bytes and modeled duration are distinct evidence.

sections.title: What Carries Forward
sourceHeadings: Slide 30: What Carries Forward
sections.body:
**`DMA`**: direct memory access.

Carry hardware-independent core and a small hardware adapter, absolute next+=period, fractional integration and bus budgeting into controllers. os_delay_until supplies the RTOS equivalent grid.

MPU6050 shares OLED wires: a 25 ms display transfer can disrupt fast sensing/control, so give display low priority and bounded page traffic.

Supported DMA offloads movement while CPU decides. Completion, ownership and error paths remain necessary.

Compose existing mechanisms around application deadlines.
